anchor.title: Sylvester Rawding Family in Front of Sod House, North of Sargent, Custer County, Nebraska
anchor.creator: Solomon D. Butcher
anchor.citation: Butcher, Solomon D. Sylvester Rawding Family in Front of Sod House, North of Sargent, Custer County, Nebraska. 1886. Photograph. Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, LOT 3026, digital ID LC-DIG-ppmsca-08372. https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/2005693378/.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph from 1886 showing the Rawding family — Sylvester, Emma, and their four children — posed in front of their sod house in Custer County, Nebraska. A mule team stands to the right, a cow grazes on the grass-covered roof, and a table set with a watermelon sits in the foreground on the open prairie.
anchor.caption: Solomon Butcher's 1886 photograph of the Rawding family in front of their Nebraska sod house — a vivid record of Homestead Act settlement on the Great Plains.

anchor.title: Tom Torlino, Navajo, Before and After
anchor.creator: John N. Choate
anchor.citation: Choate, John N. Tom Torlino, Navajo, Before and After. 1882 and 1885. Photographs. Richard Henry Pratt Papers (WA MSS S-1174), Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University. Public-domain scan via Wikimedia Commons, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tom_Torlino_Navajo_before_and_after_circa_1882.jpg.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — U.S. Copyright Expired (pre-1929 publication)
anchor.alt: Side-by-side studio portraits of Navajo student Tom Torlino. On the left, Torlino in 1882 wears traditional Navajo clothing with long hair, large earrings, and a silver necklace. On the right, Torlino in 1885 wears a dark suit and white shirt with closely cropped hair, his skin appearing lighter due to the studio lighting. Both portraits are bust-length against a plain backdrop.
anchor.caption: J. N. Choate's before-and-after studio portraits of Navajo student Tom Torlino at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School — the most widely reproduced propaganda image of federal Indian assimilation policy.

anchor.title: The Union as It Was — The Lost Cause, Worse Than Slavery
anchor.creator: Thomas Nast
anchor.citation: Nast, Thomas. "The Union as It Was — The Lost Cause, Worse Than Slavery." Harper's Weekly, October 24, 1874. Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, digital ID LC-USZ62-128619. https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/2001696840/.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: Wood engraving political cartoon showing a hooded Ku Klux Klan member shaking hands with a White League militiaman over a shield depicting an African American couple mourning their dead child. In the background, a schoolhouse burns and a lynched man hangs from a tree. The caption reads: The Union As It Was — The Lost Cause, Worse Than Slavery.
anchor.caption: Thomas Nast's October 24, 1874 Harper's Weekly cartoon indicting the Ku Klux Klan and White League for the terror campaign that ended Reconstruction.

anchor.title: The Bosses of the Senate
anchor.creator: Joseph Keppler
anchor.citation: Keppler, Joseph. "The Bosses of the Senate." Puck, January 23, 1889. Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, call number Illus. in AP101.P7 1889 (Case X). https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/2002718861/.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: Color political cartoon from 1889 depicting the U.S. Senate chamber dominated by enormous moneybag figures labeled STEEL, COPPER, OIL, IRON, SUGAR, TIN, COAL, and other industrial trusts. Tiny senators sit at desks below them. A door at the back marked PEOPLE'S ENTRANCE is bolted shut. A banner at top reads: This is the Senate of the Monopolists by the Monopolists and for the Monopolists.
anchor.caption: Joseph Keppler's January 23, 1889 Puck magazine cartoon showing industrial trusts as money-bag giants towering over tiny U.S. Senators — the Gilded Age's most famous indictment of corporate capture.

anchor.title: Next!
anchor.creator: Udo J. Keppler
anchor.citation: Keppler, Udo J. "Next!" Puck 56, no. 1436 (September 7, 1904). Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, digital ID LC-DIG-ppmsca-25884. https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/2001695241/.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: Color political cartoon from 1904 showing a giant octopus rising from a steel storage tank labeled STANDARD OIL. The octopus's tentacles wrap around a labeled state capitol, a U.S. Capitol, and buildings representing the steel, copper, and shipping industries. A fifth tentacle reaches toward the White House in the distance. The word Next! appears above the White House.
anchor.caption: Udo Keppler's September 7, 1904 Puck cartoon depicting Standard Oil as a giant octopus strangling American industry and reaching for the White House — the visual shorthand that launched Teddy Roosevelt's trust-busting.

anchor.title: Inspection Room, Ellis Island, New York
anchor.creator: Detroit Publishing Company
anchor.citation: Detroit Publishing Company. Inspection Room, Ellis Island, New York. Ca. 1910–1920. Photograph. Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, Detroit Publishing Company photograph collection, digital ID LC-DIG-det-4a24564. https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/2016812423/.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: Photograph of the interior of the Great Hall inspection room at Ellis Island, circa 1910 to 1920. American flags hang from the ceiling, tall windows line the walls, and rows of benches fill the cavernous space. The image shows the architectural scale of the federal immigration processing facility.
anchor.caption: A Detroit Publishing Company photograph of the inspection room at Ellis Island, where more than twelve million immigrants were processed between 1892 and 1954.

anchor.title: Five Cents a Spot — Unauthorized Immigrant Lodgings in a Bayard Street Tenement
anchor.creator: Jacob A. Riis
anchor.citation: Riis, Jacob A. Five Cents a Spot — Unauthorized Immigrant Lodgings in a Bayard Street Tenement. 1889. Photograph. Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, LOT 6300, digital ID cph 3a18572. https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/2002710259/.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: Black-and-white flash photograph from 1889 showing about a dozen poorly dressed men and women packed asleep on the floor and in bunks of a small, dimly lit tenement lodging room during a police raid. A metal pitcher and cookware sit on a ledge, and the walls are bare plaster lit by the photographer's flash.
anchor.caption: Jacob Riis's 1889 flash photograph of a Bayard Street lodging house, published in How the Other Half Lives (1890) — the image that forced middle-class America to see tenement poverty.
